title: From Pixels to a DataFrame: Using Pretrained YOLO to Structure a Sports Frame
text:
A picture from a soccer game holds a lot of information: where every player is standing, how close someone is to the ball, how spread out the defense is. For a human (who essentially has two GPUs as part of their prefrontal cortex) it’s easy to understand what’s going on. But for a computer it’s a grid of pixel colors embedded as numbers. The question I’m hoping to take you all through is: how do you get from a photo to a DataFrame? In a few lines of Python, we will have a pretty cool way to do this.
By the end of this post you will be able to:

use a pretrained YOLOv8 model to detect objects in an image
turn the detections into a pandas DataFrame
filter by class and confidence, then plot object locations on the image

use a pretrained YOLOv8 model to detect objects in an image
turn the detections into a pandas DataFrame
filter by class and confidence, then plot object locations on the image

title: From Pixels to a DataFrame: Using Pretrained YOLO to Structure a Sports Frame
section: What you can do with YOLO
text:
What you can do with YOLO
Object detection is a computer vision task that involves identifying and localizing objects in an image. It is a building block for many computer vision applications.
YOLO stands for “You Only Look Once” and it holds a number of object detection models. The version we’ll use, YOLOv8 from Ultralytics, comes pretrained on a dataset called COCO, which contains lots of photos which are hand-labeled. Two of the classes from COCO are exactly what we need for soccer: “person” and “sports ball”. We basically just download the weights and run the model.
For every object, it gives you three things:

a class: what the object is, such as “person”
a confidence score between 0 and 1: how sure the model is
box coordinates: the corners of a rectangle around the object, in pixels

title: From Pixels to a DataFrame: Using Pretrained YOLO to Structure a Sports Frame
text:
Step 1: Run the Model
First, install the libraries (tabulate lets pandas print Markdown tables):
pip install ultralytics pandas matplotlib tabulate
We load the model with the YOLO class from ultralytics. We’ll use YOLOv8n, the smallest and fastest of the five sizes (n, s, m, l, x). It’s also the least accurate, but for a single frame that trade-off is fine. The weights file downloads automatically the first time you run the code.

from ultralytics import YOLO
model = YOLO("yolov8n.pt")

Then we run it on our frame. model("frame.jpg") is shorthand for model.predict("frame.jpg"). It returns a list with one Results object per image, and since we passed in one image, we take [0].

result = model("frame.jpg")[0]

Here is what the model sees in our frame, plus four photos from other games. Use the arrows to click through them. The boxes around the objects are the detections from the model.


1/5: YOLO found 7 people and the ball (0.90) (confidence > 0.5).Photo: Kidsgrove Athletic v Mossley, 29 March 2025 by Dominic Nelson, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons, with detection boxes added.2/5: YOLO found 5 people and the ball (0.96) (confidence > 0.5).Photo: Shrewsbury Town practice match, 1 August 2014 by JMoore1987, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons, with detection boxes added.3/5: YOLO found 8 people and the ball (0.91) (confidence > 0.5).Photo: Leek Town v Workington, 12 April 2025 by Dominic Nelson, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons, with detection boxes added.4/5: YOLO found 5 people and the ball (0.94) (confidence > 0.5).Photo: HFX Wanderers FC vs. Forge FC by Indrid Cold, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons, with detection boxes added.5/5: YOLO found 6 people and the ball (0.92) (confidence > 0.5).Photo: Philippines vs Afghanistan, 12 September 2023 by Jethrude Hipolito, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons, with detection boxes added.

In our frame the model found 14 people and the ball, but only some of those boxes are worth keeping. The low-confidence ones are mostly small spectators behind the fence and extra boxes drawn over players it had already found. It’s pretty cool that we can just filter those lower confidence people out of the model.

title: From Pixels to a DataFrame: Using Pretrained YOLO to Structure a Sports Frame
section: Step 2: Turn the detections into a data frame
text:
Step 2: Turn the detections into a data frame
The result is a Results object, not a table. The detections live in a few parallel arrays:

result.boxes.xyxy: one row of box corners (x1, y1, x2, y2) per detection
result.boxes.conf: one confidence score per detection
result.boxes.cls: one class ID (a number) per detection
result.names: a dictionary that maps class IDs to names, such as {0: "person", 32: "sports ball"}

These line up by position, so row i of each one describes the same detection. That makes it easy to put them side by side in a DataFrame with one row per detection: the box corners (x1, y1 top-left and x2, y2 bottom-right), the class name, the confidence, and the box center (x_center, y_center).

import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame(result.boxes.xyxy, columns=["x1", "y1", "x2", "y2"])
df["class"] = [result.names[int(c)] for c in result.boxes.cls]
df["confidence"] = result.boxes.conf
df["x_center"] = (df["x1"] + df["x2"]) / 2
df["y_center"] = (df["y1"] + df["y2"]) / 2

The last two lines use the box-center equation:
\[
x_c = \frac{x_1 + x_2}{2}, \qquad y_c = \frac{y_1 + y_2}{2}
\]
This means that the center is the average of the left and right edges (for \(x\)) and the average of the top and bottom edges (for \(y\)). For plotting, we want one point per object, and the center is the natural choice.

title: From Pixels to a DataFrame: Using Pretrained YOLO to Structure a Sports Frame
text:
Step 3: Filter and plot
Now we filter the DataFrame to keep only “person” and “sports ball” detections with a confidence score above 0.5. We save the result as players so the full df stays around.

players = df[df["class"].isin(["person", "sports ball"]) & (df["confidence"] > 0.5)]
players["class"].value_counts()

class
person         7
sports ball    1
Name: count, dtype: int64


Why 0.5? YOLO’s default cutoff is 0.25, which keeps all 14 people. Raising it to 0.5 drops 7 of them: four small figures in the background and three partial or duplicate boxes. It isn’t perfect, though. Two spectators by the fence score above 0.5, and the player in white partly hidden behind the tackle scores only 0.40, so he gets cut. A cutoff is a trade-off, so check it against the image.
Finally, we plot the box centers on top of the frame:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5.5))
ax.imshow(plt.imread("frame.jpg"))
for name, group in players.groupby("class"):
    ax.scatter(group["x_center"], group["y_center"], s=60, edgecolors="white", label=name)
ax.legend()
ax.set_axis_off()
plt.show()




Centers of detections with confidence above 0.5, drawn on the original frame.




Pixel \(y\) grows downward, and imshow handles that for us. If you plot the centers without the image, call ax.invert_yaxis() or the plot comes out upside down.

title: From Pixels to a DataFrame: Using Pretrained YOLO to Structure a Sports Frame
section: A limitation: pixels are not the field
text:
A limitation: pixels are not the field
The coordinates are in pixel space, not real field positions, so distances measured in pixels are misleading. Two players 100 px apart near the camera are much closer together on the field than two players 100 px apart far from the camera. A homography fixes that by mapping pixels to field coordinates using at least four points whose real positions you know, like the corners of the penalty box. Our frame doesn’t show enough field markings for that, but it’s the next step if you want distances in meters.

title: From Pixels to a DataFrame: Using Pretrained YOLO to Structure a Sports Frame
text:
Conclusion and next steps
We went from a photo to a table: run a pretrained YOLO model on the image, pull the detections into a DataFrame, filter by class and confidence, and plot the results. Once the frame is a DataFrame, all of the usual pandas tools apply. You can count players, find who is closest to the ball, or measure how spread out a team is. Run the model on every frame of a video and stack the DataFrames, and you can start tracking how players move.
Try it yourself: Feel free to use this code and run the model yourself! It should work really well for most sports since most sports have a ball and players.

title: What Makes a Hugging Face Model Popular? Building a Dataset of the 3,000 Most Downloaded Models
text:
I’m really into machine learning, and Hugging Face is basically where everyone shares open models. Every model page shows a download count and a like count, and I think those two numbers are a pretty honest signal of what people actually use, not just what gets hype. So I wanted a dataset of the most downloaded models with enough features to ask a simple question:
Does a model’s task, library, license, or size have anything to do with how popular it is?
A second question came up once I had the data: are downloads and likes even measuring the same thing?
The code and the dataset are in the hf-model-popularity repo.

title: What Makes a Hugging Face Model Popular? Building a Dataset of the 3,000 Most Downloaded Models
text:
I’m really into machine learning, and Hugging Face is basically where everyone shares open models. Every model page shows a download count and a like count, and I think those two numbers are a pretty honest signal of what people actually use, not just what gets hype. So I wanted a dataset of the most downloaded models with enough features to ask a simple question:
Does a model’s task, library, license, or size have anything to do with how popular it is?
A second question came up once I had the data: are downloads and likes even measuring the same thing?
The code and the dataset are in the hf-model-popularity repo.

title: What Makes a Hugging Face Model Popular? Building a Dataset of the 3,000 Most Downloaded Models
text:
Is this allowed?
Before writing any code I checked three things:

robots.txt is one line, Allow: /.
The Hub API docs say the endpoint I used is public and doesn’t need a token. The rate limit page says 500 requests per 5 minutes, and the response headers tell you how many you have left.
The arXiv API is free and asks for about 3 seconds between requests.

The data is about models, not people. The only person-like field is the author, which is a public username or org name. There are no model weights and no user data, so I felt fine putting the CSV in the repo. I also sent a User-Agent that names the project and links to the repo so anyone on their end can tell what the traffic is.

title: What Makes a Hugging Face Model Popular? Building a Dataset of the 3,000 Most Downloaded Models
text:
How to get the data
It’s three scripts, and you don’t need an API key for either source.

1. One request per 1,000 models
My original plan was to list the top models and then hit the detail endpoint 3,000 times to get the license and parameter count. It turns out you don’t need to. The list endpoint has an expand[] parameter that adds those fields to the same call, and limit goes up to 1,000, so the whole thing is 3 requests.
params = {
    "sort": "downloads", "direction": -1, "limit": 1000,
    "expand[]": ["author", "pipeline_tag", "library_name", "tags", "cardData",
                 "downloads", "downloadsAllTime", "likes", "createdAt",
                 "lastModified", "safetensors", "gated"],
}
response = session.get("https://huggingface.co/api/models", params=params)
next_url = response.links["next"]["url"]   # pagination comes from the Link header
Two things tripped me up. Pagination is a Link header instead of a field in the JSON (requests parses it for you as response.links), and the license isn’t its own field. It’s in tags as license:apache-2.0, so you pull it out of the tag list.
I save the raw JSON exactly as it came back, plus one flattened row per model. That way if I want a different field later I don’t have to hit the API again.


2. Look up the papers
About half of the models have tags like arxiv:1908.10084. The arXiv API takes a comma-separated id_list, so I sent 100 IDs per request (8 requests total, 3 seconds apart) and parsed the Atom XML with the standard library. That gives each paper’s date and primary category (cs.CL, cs.CV, and so on).


3. Clean
The cleaning script joins the two raw files and makes the decisions I didn’t want to make while collecting:

329 models (11%) have a creation date of exactly 2022-03-02. That’s the day the Hub migrated, not a real date, so I blank it out and keep a created_at_known flag.
Parameter counts come from safetensors metadata, and 1,168 models don’t have it. I left those missing instead of guessing.
Each model gets its earliest paper’s date and category, a size bucket, and likes per million downloads.

Everything is really skewed. The median model has about 2.2 million all-time downloads and 58 likes, but the top model (sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2) has 4.2 billion downloads on its own, which is 6.6% of all the downloads in the dataset. The top 10 models have 28%. So everything below uses medians and log scales.
The most common tasks are text-generation (577 models), image-text-to-text (382), and token-classification (354). That last one is mostly one org. OpenMed uploaded 237 medical NER models on a single day in July 2025, and 315 of the top 3,000 models are theirs.

title: What Makes a Hugging Face Model Popular? Building a Dataset of the 3,000 Most Downloaded Models
text:
What I found

Downloads and likes are measuring different things
The correlation between log likes and log downloads is only 0.42. Grouping by task shows why.


Code
by_task = models.groupby("task").agg(n=("model_id", "size"), median_downloads=("downloads_all_time", "median"), median_likes=("likes", "median"))
by_task["median_downloads"] = by_task["median_downloads"] / 1e6
by_task = by_task[by_task["n"] >= 30]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 5))
by_task.sort_values("median_downloads").plot.barh(y="median_downloads", ax=axes[0], color=BLUE, legend=False, width=0.6)
axes[0].set_title("Median all-time downloads (millions)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("")
by_task.sort_values("median_likes").plot.barh(y="median_likes", ax=axes[1], color=ORANGE, legend=False, width=0.6)
axes[1].set_title("Median likes")
axes[1].set_ylabel("")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()





Median all-time downloads and median likes by task, for tasks with at least 30 models.




The most downloaded task is fill-mask (median 18.6 million), which is BERT and models like it. They’re old and small and get pulled into a ton of pipelines, but hardly anyone likes them. The most liked tasks are image-to-image (median 405) and text-to-image (210), which are the ones people actually play with.
The extremes make it even more obvious. The models with the fewest likes per download are things like vllm-project/tiny-random-LlamaForCausalLM (2 likes, 26 million downloads). Those are tiny test models that CI pipelines download over and over, so a lot of the download count is automation and not people.


Bigger models get more likes but not more downloads


Code
has_size = models[models["num_parameters"] > 0]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5.5))
ax.scatter(has_size["num_parameters"], has_size["downloads_all_time"], s=5 + has_size["likes"] / 40,
           color=BLUE, alpha=0.35, edgecolors="white", linewidths=0.5)
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("Parameters")
ax.set_ylabel("All-time downloads")
ax.set_title("Downloads are flat across model size")
for _, row in has_size.nlargest(4, "likes").iterrows():
    ax.annotate(row["model_id"].split("/")[-1], (row["num_parameters"], row["downloads_all_time"]),
                fontsize=8, color=GRAY, xytext=(5, 5), textcoords="offset points")
plt.show()





Parameters vs all-time downloads for the 1,832 models with a parameter count, both axes log. Point size is likes.




The correlation between log parameters and log downloads is actually slightly negative (-0.11). Median downloads are about the same in every size bucket (2.3 to 3.8 million), and the smallest bucket is the highest. Likes are different. The median goes from 12 likes for models under 100M parameters to 162 for models over 10B, with a correlation of 0.43. So people like the big flagship models but run the small ones.


Library and license mostly tell you who made the model
transformers is 55% of the dataset. diffusers models have the highest median likes (265) since they’re image models. For license, 55% are apache-2.0 and 14% are MIT, and apache-2.0 models have the lowest median likes (46). The licenses with the most likes are other and gemma, which really just means a big lab wrote its own license. Gated models are the same story. There are only 89 of them, but they have a median of 1,137 likes compared to 54 for everything else. Gating is something Meta and Google do, so it’s tracking the lab more than anything.


The newer models are generation models


Code
top_tasks = models["task"].value_counts().head(5).index
by_year = models[models["task"].isin(top_tasks)].groupby(["created_year", "task"]).size().unstack("task")[top_tasks]
ax = by_year.plot.bar(figsize=(9, 5), color=[BLUE, ORANGE, "#1baf7a", "#eda100", "#e87ba4"], width=0.8, edgecolor="white")
ax.set_xlabel("Year created")
ax.set_ylabel("Models")
ax.set_title("New models in the top 3,000 are mostly text and image-text generation")
ax.set_xticklabels([int(y) for y in by_year.index], rotation=0)
ax.legend(title="", frameon=False)
plt.show()





Models created per year among the top 3,000, five most common tasks. Models with the placeholder 2022-03-02 date are left out, and 2026 only runs through November 4.




Almost a third of the top 3,000 (978) were created in 2026, and they’re mostly text-generation and image-text-to-text. The older tasks like fill-mask and sentence-similarity still get downloaded a ton, but almost nothing new in those categories makes it into the top 3,000. On the paper side, half the models link an arXiv paper, cs.CL papers outnumber cs.CV 903 to 329, and the median gap from paper to model is 76 days. About a quarter of the models were on the Hub before their paper was.

title: What Makes a Hugging Face Model Popular? Building a Dataset of the 3,000 Most Downloaded Models
text:
Caveats

The top 3,000 by 30-day downloads is a small slice of a Hub with millions of models, so everything here is about the winners.
Downloads count CI runs and automated pipelines, not just people.
11% of the creation dates and 39% of the parameter counts are missing, and it isn’t random (older models and non-safetensors formats).
Downloads and likes change every day, so a rerun will give you different numbers.

title: What Makes a Hugging Face Model Popular? Building a Dataset of the 3,000 Most Downloaded Models
text:
Try it yourself
Everything is in the repo: the three scripts, the raw API output, the processed CSV, and a longer EDA. Run uv sync and then the scripts in order. If you want to go further, the same API works for datasets and Spaces, and the huggingface_hub package wraps all of it if you’d rather not deal with the pagination yourself.
